38696:
2 Thessalonians is soaked in Jewish prophetic and apocalyptic imagery. The Lord Jesus is 'revealed from heaven with his mighty angels in flaming fire, inflicting vengeance' (2 Thess 1:7-8), language borrowed from Isaiah's descriptions of the LORD coming in fire (Isa 66:15). Those who do not know God will be away 'from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his might' (2 Thess 1:9), almost word for word from Isaiah 2:10 in the Greek Old Testament, where people hide from the terror of the LORD. Once again, texts about Israel's God are applied to Jesus.

The man of lawlessness sitting in God's temple recalls Daniel's 'abomination of desolation' (Dan 9:27, Dan 11:31, Dan 11:36) and Jesus' warning about the same (Mark 13:14). For a Jewish audience these were memories of real profanations: Antiochus IV setting up a pagan altar in the temple, Pompey entering the holy of holies in 63 BC, and Caligula's statue plan. The 'restrainer' may also draw on Jewish ideas that God delays the end until appointed things are complete.

Readers disagree whether 'the temple of God' means the literal Jerusalem temple (standing when Paul wrote, if he did), a future rebuilt temple (the dispensational view), or the church (as Augustine and some Reformers suggested). The letter itself is more concerned with faithfulness than with timetables: God will be faithful to his suffering people, and they are to stand firm in what they were taught.
38698: Their faith and love are growing despite affliction.
38700: When Jesus is revealed, oppressors will be repaid and the afflicted given rest and glory.
38702: Do not be shaken: the rebellion and the man of lawlessness must come first.
38704: Something holds lawlessness back for now; the Lord Jesus will destroy the lawless one by his coming.
38706: God chose them for salvation; hold to the traditions taught by word or letter.
38708: Pray for the mission, avoid the idle, imitate Paul's labour, and warn rather than hate the disobedient.
38709: Stand firm until the day of the Lord
38730: The prophets' day of God's decisive judgement and salvation, now linked to the coming of the Lord Jesus.
38732: Defiant rebellion against God. 'The man of lawlessness' embodies it.
38734: Something (neuter) and someone (masculine) holding back the lawless one. Its identity is unknown to us and widely debated.
38736: Originally soldiers out of rank; here members who refused to work and disrupted community life.
38738: Teachings handed on from the apostles, in speech and in writing.
38739: The two letters share structure and phrases; the second corrects misuse of the first's teaching on the day of the Lord.
38740: The arrogant ruler who exalts himself above every god and profanes the temple is Daniel's figure.
38741: The Lord coming in fire and the Messiah slaying the wicked with the breath of his lips come from Isaiah.
38742: Jesus' warning about the desolating sacrilege and false messiahs parallels this teaching.
38743: The 'antichrist' tradition in John's letters is often linked with the man of lawlessness.
38744: Jesus is the judge who will be 'revealed from heaven' and the one in whose name and by whose grace believers are glorified (2 Thess 1:7, 2 Thess 1:12). He will slay the lawless one 'with the breath of his mouth', the messianic King's work from Isaiah 11:4. Christian tradition has used this letter to speak of an antichrist figure; Jewish readers recognise in it the familiar pattern of an arrogant tyrant defeated by God's anointed. The letter's comfort lies in Christ's certain victory, not in identifying the villain.
38745: 'If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat' (2 Thess 3:10) as a rule against welfare
38746: 2 Thessalonians 3:10 teaches that people who do not work should not receive help; it is quoted in debates against government welfare or charity to the unemployed.
38747: Paul addresses specific church members who were able to work but refused, probably out of end-time excitement or reliance on wealthy patrons, and were living off the community's shared meals. He says 'not willing', not 'not able'. In the same breath he urges believers not to grow weary in doing good (2 Thess 3:13) and to treat the idle as brothers to be warned, not enemies. Scholars such as Bruce Winter and Jeffrey Weima link the problem to patron-client dependency.
38748: Evangelical commentators agree that the verse is about the church's internal discipline of able-bodied people refusing work, not a policy statement about the state or about those who cannot find work. Some argue it does express a wider principle of responsibility that can inform social ethics, which is fair as long as the 'not willing' condition and the call to keep doing good remain.
38749: Used out of context, the verse can justify neglect of the poor; in context it protects a generous community from exploitation while keeping it generous.
38750: Identifying the man of lawlessness with current figures
38751: The man of lawlessness is the Antichrist, and Christians should watch the news to identify him; at different times he has been identified with the pope, Napoleon, Hitler, various politicians or a coming world leader.
38752: Paul says the Thessalonians already knew what he had taught (2 Thess 2:5-6). His purpose is to calm a church that was 'shaken' by end-time claims, not to supply a code for future decoding. Interpreters from Augustine onwards admitted they did not know what the restrainer was. Scholars across traditions (Malherbe, Weima, Fee) stress that the passage drew on figures known from Daniel and recent history.
38753: Many evangelicals, especially dispensationalists, hold that Paul does predict a future individual who will appear before Christ's return, so watchfulness is warranted. Most evangelical commentators nonetheless warn against date-setting and naming individuals, which has repeatedly failed. The debate concerns whether the fulfilment is future, past or symbolic; the error is speculative identification.
38754: Speculation has damaged the church's credibility and fuelled hostility toward groups cast as the Antichrist. The text's own aim is steadiness.
38755: A suffering church was assured of God's justice, protected from panic about the end, and reminded that faithful waiting means ordinary work and mutual care.
38756: 2 Thessalonians speaks to believers facing injustice, to communities swept up in end-times speculation, and to churches balancing generosity with responsibility.
38757: A charge to Paul's trusted delegate in Ephesus to stop false teaching and order God's household so that the church can stand as a pillar of the truth in its city.
38758: Presented as Paul writing to Timothy, his 'true child in the faith' (1 Tim 1:2), whom he had left in Ephesus while he went on to Macedonia (1 Tim 1:3). If pseudonymous, a later follower of Paul applied his teaching to the needs of churches around 90-120.
38759: The letter names Paul and refers to his conversion as persecutor turned apostle (1 Tim 1:12-16). Polycarp (c. 110-135) seems to echo it, and Irenaeus (c. 180) quotes it as Paul's. Many critical scholars (Martin Dibelius, Raymond Collins) judge the Pastorals pseudonymous because about a third of their vocabulary is absent from the other Pauline letters, the church order seems more developed, and the journeys do not fit Acts. Defenders (Luke Timothy Johnson, William Mounce, Philip Towner) point to the use of a secretary, the different purpose of letters to a delegate, and a release from Rome after Acts 28.
38761: Paul says he urged Timothy to remain in Ephesus 'when I was going to Macedonia' (1 Tim 1:3). This journey does not clearly match Acts, so if Pauline it is usually placed after a release from Rome. The exact city is not named; Thessalonica is used for the map point.
38762: Timothy, and through him the church in Ephesus
38763: Some teachers, apparently from within the church's own leadership, were promoting 'myths and endless genealogies', speculative uses of the Law, ascetic bans on marriage and some foods (1 Tim 4:3), and possibly the belief that the resurrection had already happened (compare 2 Tim 2:18). Hymenaeus and Alexander had been put out (1 Tim 1:20). Wealth, widows' support and the selection of leaders were all causing problems.
38764: Paul arrives in Rome as a prisoner (Acts 28:16).
38765: End of Paul's two-year house arrest where Acts stops (Acts 28:30); later tradition says he was released and travelled further.
38766: Traditional date for 1 Timothy if written by Paul between imprisonments.
38767: 1 Clement says Paul reached 'the limit of the west' before his death (1 Clement 5.7), which some read as Spain and as evidence for a release.
38768: Polycarp's letter to the Philippians appears to echo 1 Timothy 6:7-10, showing the letter was known by then (approximate date).
38769:
Ephesus was the great city of Roman Asia, dominated by the temple of Artemis, whose cult employed many priestesses and attracted pilgrims, and full of competing philosophies, magic and mystery religions. The church there had begun in Paul's long ministry (Acts 19) and by the time of this letter had elders (Acts 20:17), several house churches, wealthy members and a system for supporting widows.

Paul had predicted to the Ephesian elders that 'from among your own selves will arise men speaking twisted things' (Acts 20:30). 1 Timothy shows that happening. The false teaching is hard to reconstruct but seems to combine Jewish-flavoured speculation (genealogies, wanting to be 'teachers of the law', 1 Tim 1:4-7), ascetic rules, and an elitist claim to 'knowledge' (gnōsis, 1 Tim 6:20). The teachers seem to have used religion for financial gain (1 Tim 6:5) and to have found an audience among some women, perhaps younger widows going from house to house (1 Tim 5:13; compare 2 Tim 3:6).

The letter's answer is not a full theology but a practical order for 'the household of God' (1 Tim 3:15). Leaders must be people of proven character, with qualities that outsiders also respect. The church should pray for rulers, so that believers can live peaceful lives. Widows truly alone should be supported by the church, others by their families. The rich should be generous. Underlying everything is concern for the church's reputation in a city that watched it closely, and for the 'sound' (healthy) teaching centred on Christ Jesus who came to save sinners (1 Tim 1:15).
38770: The household as the model of community
38771: Ancient households included extended family, slaves and clients under a head. The church is called 'the household of God', so its leaders must manage their own households well, and its order mirrors familiar household relationships.
38773: A woman without husband or sons often had no means of support. Jewish law commanded care for widows (Deut 14:29), and the church had a list of enrolled widows who served in prayer and good works. 1 Timothy sets criteria to protect both widows and the church's resources.
38775: Leaders must be 'above reproach' and well thought of by outsiders, because the church's honour, and the gospel's credibility, depended on how its members appeared in the city.
38777: Elaborate hairstyles, gold and expensive clothes signalled wealth and sometimes sexual availability among Roman elite women; the 'new Roman woman' of the period was criticised by moralists. Instruction on dress addresses status display in worship.
38779: Philosophers debated contentment (autarkeia). 1 Timothy redirects it: godliness with contentment is great gain, and the wealthy should be rich in good works, using money as benefactors who store up treasure in God's future.
38781: Many church members were slaves, some owned by believers. The letter tells believing slaves to honour masters so the gospel is not slandered, which shows a missionary concern within, not a challenge to, the social order.
38782:
1 Timothy's world is a Gentile city, but its theology is Jewish. Its central confession is the Shema extended: 'there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus' (1 Tim 2:5). Its prayers 'for kings and all who are in high positions' (1 Tim 2:1-2) follow the Jewish practice of praying for the rulers of the lands of exile (Jer 29:7) and for the emperor, which Jews offered daily in the temple instead of worshipping him. Its blessing of God as 'the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God' (1 Tim 1:17) and 'King of kings and Lord of lords' (1 Tim 6:15) sound like synagogue doxologies. Care for widows, the payment of elders (with Deut 25:4 quoted in 1 Tim 5:18) and the requirement of two or three witnesses (Deut 19:15, 1 Tim 5:19) all draw directly on Torah.

The letter says 'the law is good, if one uses it lawfully' (1 Tim 1:8). The false teachers' misuse of the Law and their 'genealogies' may reflect a speculative interpretation of Genesis, possibly with Jewish elements, but the letter does not oppose the Law itself; it says the Law exists to restrain wrongdoing (1 Tim 1:9-10), a list that follows the order of the Ten Commandments.

Scholars of the 'Paul within Judaism' school have written less about the Pastorals, partly because most of them think the Pastorals are post-Pauline and reflect a church that was becoming more Gentile and more settled. Traditional scholars who accept Pauline authorship see the same Jewish Paul at work here as in Romans, now applying his gospel to church order.
38784: Timothy must silence speculative teaching; the goal is love from a pure heart.
38786: Christ came to save sinners, and Paul is exhibit A of his patience.
38788: Pray for all, because God desires all to be saved; men pray without anger; women adorn themselves with good works and learn quietly.
38790: Overseers and deacons must be tested, faithful and respected; the church is the pillar of truth, centred on the mystery of godliness.
38792: Reject ascetic myths, train in godliness, read Scripture publicly and let no one despise your youth.
38794: Treat members as family; support real widows, honour and discipline elders fairly, guide slaves.
38796: The love of money ruins; the rich must be generous. Guard the deposit.
38797: Order in God's household for the sake of truth
38818: Reverent devotion shown in a whole way of life. A common Greco-Roman virtue word, used ten times in 1 Timothy for life shaped by the gospel.
38820: Teaching that produces spiritual health, as opposed to diseased, quarrelsome speculation.
38822: A supervising leader, later the word for 'bishop'. Here seemingly overlapping with elders (presbyteroi).
38824: Both personal trust and 'the faith', the content of what is believed and to be guarded.
38826: Something entrusted for safekeeping, like money left with a banker; here the gospel entrusted to Timothy.
38827: Paul's farewell to the Ephesian elders warns of false teachers arising among them.
38828: Titus gives almost the same qualifications for elders and the same concern about myths.
38829: The second letter shows Paul's final charge to Timothy and names some of the same opponents.
38830: Torah rules on oxen, witnesses and widows ground church practice.
38831: The appeal to Adam and Eve in the instruction on women draws on Genesis 2-3; how it does so is debated.
38832: 'The labourer deserves his wages' is quoted as Scripture alongside Deuteronomy and matches Jesus' words in Luke.
38833: Christ Jesus 'came into the world to save sinners' (1 Tim 1:15), is the 'one mediator between God and men' who 'gave himself as a ransom for all' (1 Tim 2:5-6), and made 'the good confession' before Pontius Pilate (1 Tim 6:13). The early hymn of 1 Tim 3:16 traces his story from being 'manifested in the flesh' to being 'taken up in glory'. Christians read these as compressed creeds. Jewish readers will notice that the one mediator is described as 'the man Christ Jesus', firmly within a framework where God remains one.
38834: 1 Timothy 2:11-15: universal ban, or a specific Ephesian problem?
38835: Two popular positions face each other. One: 1 Tim 2:12 plainly forbids any woman to teach or exercise authority over men in church, and this is God's permanent order grounded in creation. The other: the verse was only about uneducated Ephesian women and has no relevance today.
38836: Scholars note several features. The verb authentein (2:12) occurs only here in the New Testament, and its meaning (to exercise authority, to domineer, to instigate) is disputed. The false teaching was spreading among some women (1 Tim 5:13-15). Women were to 'learn', which was itself progressive. Verse 15, 'she will be saved through childbearing', is one of the hardest verses in the New Testament. Egalitarian scholars (Philip Payne, Craig Keener, Linda Belleville, Gordon Fee) read the restriction as addressing a local crisis of women spreading false teaching; some link it to Artemis-related ideas, though that link is debated.
38837: Complementarian scholars (Douglas Moo, Thomas Schreiner, Andreas Köstenberger, D. A. Carson) argue that the grounds Paul gives are not local but creational: Adam was formed first, then Eve (1 Tim 2:13), so the restriction applies to authoritative teaching of the gathered church today. Köstenberger's study of the sentence structure argues that 'teach' and 'exercise authority' are both positive activities. They reject any reading that bars women from all teaching or treats women as inferior. This is a genuine, unresolved scholarly debate; both sides in their best forms reject the dismissive popular extremes. See /debates/gender-roles.
38838: The passage determines who may preach and lead in many churches. Understanding both readings at their best helps believers disagree with integrity.
38839: 'Money is the root of all evil'
38840: A popular saying, often attributed to the Bible, is that money itself is the root of all evil, so wealth is suspect in itself.
38841: The verse says 'the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils' (1 Tim 6:10). It warns those who 'desire to be rich' (1 Tim 6:9). The same chapter tells the rich not to give up their wealth but to be generous and rich in good works (1 Tim 6:17-19). The concern is greed and its power to pull people away from the faith, a theme shared with Jewish wisdom and with moral philosophers of the time.
38842: There is little scholarly dispute; all agree on the wording. The opposite error, treating wealth as a sign of God's favour, is just as far from the text.
38843: The verse is about the heart's loyalty and the use of wealth, not a ban on having money.
38844: A church in a great city, troubled by persuasive insiders and by money, received a practical pattern for leadership, worship and care that would make it trustworthy before its neighbours.
38845: 1 Timothy is still the main text for choosing church leaders by character rather than charisma, for church care of the vulnerable, and for warnings about greed. Its gender passages remain among the most debated in the Bible.
38846: Paul's farewell from a Roman prison: a dying mentor urges his spiritual son not to be ashamed, to suffer with him, to hold to Scripture and to pass the faith on to others.
38847: Presented as Paul in his final imprisonment in Rome, expecting execution (2 Tim 4:6). He writes to Timothy, whose grandmother Lois and mother Eunice had taught him the faith (2 Tim 1:5).
38848: The letter claims Paul and is full of specific personal detail: a cloak left at Troas with Carpus, books and parchments (2 Tim 4:13), Demas deserting, Luke alone remaining, Alexander the coppersmith doing harm. Many who doubt the Pastorals see these as literary colour; others, including some critical scholars (Jerome Murphy-O'Connor, Michael Prior), think 2 Timothy differs from 1 Timothy and Titus and may be genuine. Conservative scholars accept all three.
38850: Onesiphorus searched for Paul in Rome and found him (2 Tim 1:17). This seems a harsher imprisonment than the house arrest of Acts 28: Paul is chained like a criminal (2 Tim 2:9) and has had a first hearing at which no one supported him (2 Tim 4:16).
38852: Paul greets Priscilla and Aquila and the household of Onesiphorus, who were associated with Ephesus, and mentions sending Tychicus there (2 Tim 4:12, 2 Tim 4:19). Timothy faces teachers like Hymenaeus and Philetus, who say the resurrection has already happened, and may be tempted to timidity and shame over Paul's chains.
38853: Great Fire of Rome; Nero blames the Christians and executes many (Tacitus, Annals 15.44).
38854: Jewish revolt against Rome begins in Judea.
38855: Approximate traditional date of Paul's beheading in Rome under Nero (Eusebius, Church History 2.25), the setting of 2 Timothy if authentic.
38856: Nero commits suicide; the year of the four emperors follows in 69.
38857: 1 Clement recalls Paul's chains, exile and martyrdom (1 Clement 5).
38858:
2 Timothy is written in the form of a farewell testament, a well-known Jewish genre in which a dying leader gives final instructions to his successor: Jacob to his sons (Gen 49), Moses to Joshua and Israel (Deut 31-33), David to Solomon (1 Kgs 2:1-9). Like those, it reviews the leader's life, warns of hard times ahead and hands on a charge. It also has the warmth of Greco-Roman friendship letters, with requests for visits and personal news.

The circumstances look grim. Christians in Rome had become targets after the fire of 64, when Tacitus says Nero punished them with horrible cruelty. Being associated with a chained prisoner brought shame and danger, which explains why 'all who are in Asia turned away' (2 Tim 1:15) and why Paul praises Onesiphorus for not being ashamed of his chains (2 Tim 1:16). Prisoners depended on friends for food, clothing and company; Paul asks for his cloak before winter (2 Tim 4:13, 2 Tim 4:21). Only Luke is with him.

The false teaching in Asia seems to be the same as in 1 Timothy, with a new detail: Hymenaeus and Philetus said 'the resurrection has already happened' (2 Tim 2:18), perhaps a spiritualised view that believers already live a risen life, making the body and the future irrelevant. Paul's answer is to look forward to 'that day' (2 Tim 1:12, 2 Tim 4:8) and to keep the gospel safe by entrusting it 'to faithful men who will be able to teach others also' (2 Tim 2:2), four generations in one verse.
38860: Imprisonment was a public disgrace and imprisoned people relied on visitors. Paul's repeated 'do not be ashamed' addresses the social cost of standing with him.
38862: A Jewish and Greco-Roman genre of last words: reviewing one's life, warning of the future, and charging a successor. 2 Timothy follows this pattern.
38864: Teachers and students formed fictive-kin bonds. Timothy is Paul's 'beloved child', and the faith passes along family lines: from Lois to Eunice to Timothy, and from Paul to Timothy to others.
38866: Three standard images from moral philosophy for disciplined effort and delayed reward.
38868: A libation of wine poured on a sacrifice, and the victor's wreath at the games, picture Paul's death as worship and his life as a completed race.
38870: Papyrus scrolls and parchment notebooks were expensive; Paul's request suggests he was still studying and writing. Some suggest the parchments contained Scripture or his own notes.
